San Francisco has a population of 808,988 residents as of 2023.
San Francisco is the fourth most populous city in the U.S. state of California behind Los Angeles, San Diego, and San Jose.
San Francisco covers a land area of 46.9 square miles (121 square kilometers).
San Francisco is the second-most densely populated major U.S. city behind New York City.
Among the 92 U.S. cities proper with over 250,000 residents, San Francisco is ranked first by per capita income and sixth by aggregate income as of 2022.
The San Jose–San Francisco–Oakland, CA CSA is the 5th largest in the nation, with an approximate population of over 9,010,244.
Prior to European settlement, the modern city proper was inhabited by the Yelamu, who spoke a language now referred to as Ramaytush Ohlone.
On June 29, 1776, settlers from New Spain established the Presidio of San Francisco at the Golden Gate and the Mission San Francisco de Asís a few miles away, both named for Francis of Assisi.

The California gold rush of 1849 brought rapid growth, transforming an unimportant hamlet into a busy port, making it the largest city on the West Coast at the time; between 1870 and 1900, approximately one quarter of California's population resided in the city proper.
In 1856, San Francisco became a consolidated city-county.
After three-quarters of the city was destroyed by the 1906 earthquake and fire, it was quickly rebuilt, hosting the Panama–Pacific International Exposition nine years later.
In World War II, it was a major port of embarkation for naval service members shipping out to the Pacific Theater.

In 1945, the United Nations Charter was signed in San Francisco, establishing the United Nations and in 1951, the Treaty of San Francisco re-established peaceful relations between Japan and the Allied Powers.

After the war, the confluence of returning servicemen, significant immigration, liberalizing attitudes, the rise of the beatnik and hippie countercultures, the sexual revolution, the peace movement growing from opposition to United States involvement in the Vietnam War, and other factors led to the Summer of Love and the gay rights movement, cementing San Francisco as a center of liberal activism in the United States.

San Francisco and the surrounding San Francisco Bay Area are a global center of economic activity and the arts and sciences, spurred by leading universities, high-tech, healthcare, finance, insurance, real estate, and professional services sectors.

As of 2020[update], the metropolitan area, with 6.7 million residents, ranked 5th by GDP ($874 billion) and 2nd by GDP per capita ($131,082) across the OECD countries, ahead of global cities like Paris, London, and Singapore.

San Francisco anchors the 13th most populous metropolitan statistical area in the United States with 4.6 million residents, and the fourth-largest by aggregate income and economic output, with a GDP of $729 billion in 2022[update].

The wider San Jose–San Francisco–Oakland Combined Statistical Area is the nation's fifth-most populous, with around nine million residents, and the third-largest by economic output, with a GDP of $1.32 trillion in 2022[update].
In the same year, San Francisco proper had a GDP of $252.2 billion, and a GDP per capita of $312,000.
San Francisco was ranked fifth in the world and second in the United States on the Global Financial Centres Index as of September 2023[update].

Despite a continuing exodus of businesses from the downtown area of San Francisco, the city is still home to numerous companies inside and outside of technology, including Salesforce, Uber, Airbnb, Levi's, Gap, Dropbox, and Lyft.

In 2022, San Francisco had more than 1.7 million international visitors – the fifth-most visited city from abroad in the United States after New York City, Miami, Orlando, and Los Angeles – and approximately 20 million domestic visitors for a total of 21.9 million visitors.

The city is known for its steep rolling hills and eclectic mix of architecture across varied neighborhoods, as well as its cooling summers, fog, and notable landmarks, including the Golden Gate Bridge, cable cars, and Alcatraz, along with the Chinatown and Mission districts.

The city is home to a number of educational and cultural institutions, such as the University of California, San Francisco, the University of San Francisco, San Francisco State University, the San Francisco Conservatory of Music, the de Young Museum, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the San Francisco Symphony, the San Francisco Ballet, the San Francisco Opera, the SFJAZZ Center, and the California Academy of Sciences.
Two major league sports teams, the San Francisco Giants and the Golden State Warriors, play their home games within San Francisco proper.

San Francisco International Airport (SFO) offers flights to over 125 destinations, while a light rail and bus network, in tandem with the BART and Caltrain systems, connects nearly every part of San Francisco with the wider region.
San Francisco takes its name from Mission San Francisco de Asís.

The city has officially been known as San Francisco since 1847 when Washington Allon Bartlett, then serving as the city's alcalde, renamed it from Yerba Buena (Spanish for "Good Herb"), which had been used throughout the Spanish and Mexican eras since approximately 1776.
The name Yerba Buena continues to be used in locations such as on Yerba Buena Island and in the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts and Yerba Buena Gardens.
For a chronological guide, see Timeline of San Francisco.
The earliest archeological evidence of human habitation of the territory of San Francisco dates to 3000 BCE.
The Yelamu group of the Ramaytush people resided in a few small villages when an overland Spanish exploration party arrived on November 2, 1769.
Juan Bautista de Anza established the Presidio of San Francisco for the Spanish Empire in 1776.
Mission San Francisco de Asís was founded by Padre Francisco Palóu on October 9, 1776.
The Spanish Empire claimed San Francisco as part of Las Californias, a province of the Viceroyalty of New Spain.
Juana Briones de Miranda, known as the "Founding Mother of San Francisco," built her rancho near El Polín Spring in 1833 and founded the first civilian household in San Francisco.
In 1846, the Battle of Yerba Buena was an early U.S. victory in the American conquest of California.
The California gold rush brought a flood of treasure seekers (known as "forty-niners") to San Francisco over rival Benicia, raising the population from 1,000 in 1848 to 25,000 by December 1849.
San Francisco County was one of the state's 18 original counties established at California statehood in 1850.
The Bank of California, established in 1863, was the first commercial bank in Western United States.
Development of the Port of San Francisco and establishment of overland access to the eastern U.S. rail system via the newly completed Pacific Railroad helped make the Bay Area a center for trade.
The 1906 San Francisco earthquake was the deadliest in U.S. history.
Rebuilding was rapid and performed on a grand scale, with Amadeo Giannini's Bank of Italy providing loans to many whose livelihoods had been devastated.
Urban planning projects in the 1950s and 1960s involved widespread destruction and redevelopment of west-side neighborhoods.
The Bay Bridge under construction on Yerba Buena Island in 1935 was a major civil engineering project that completed with the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge and Golden Gate Bridge.
San Francisco is located on the West Coast of the United States, at the north end of the San Francisco Peninsula.
There are more than 50 hills within the city limits.
Lake Merced, located in southwestern San Francisco, remains protected in what is essentially its original form.
The historic center of San Francisco is the northeast quadrant anchored by Market Street and the waterfront.
The Western Addition neighborhood became established with a large African American population after World War II.
Pacific Heights features homes built by wealthy San Franciscans following the 1906 earthquake.

The Mission District, populated in the 19th century by Californios and working-class immigrants from Germany, Ireland, Italy, and Scandinavia, saw significant redevelopment following the construction of Oracle Park.
San Francisco has a warm-summer Mediterranean climate with moist winters and dry summers.
Temperatures reach or exceed 80°F on an average of only 21 days a year at downtown San Francisco International Airport (SFO).
Historically, tule elk were present in San Francisco County based on archaeological evidence.
The 2020 United States census showed San Francisco's population to be 873,965.
San Francisco is part of the five-county San Francisco–Oakland–Hayward, CA Metropolitan Statistical Area with a region of 4.7 million people (13th most populous in the U.S.).

As of the 2020 census, the racial makeup included: Whites (41.3%), Asians (33.9%), African Americans (5.3%), Multiracial Americans (9.9%), Native Americans and Alaska Natives (0.7%), Native Hawaiians and other Pacific Islanders (0.4%), and persons of other races (8.4%).
The principal Hispanic groups in the city were those of Mexican (7%) and Salvadoran (2%) ancestry.
San Francisco has a diversified service economy with employment spread across professional services.

Approximately 27% of workers are employed in professional business services; 14% in leisure and hospitality; 13% in government services; 12% in education and health care; 11% in trade, transportation, and utilities; and 8% in financial activities.
San Francisco's Financial District is still considered the Wall Street of the West.
The city has a diversified service economy with employment spread across professional services, including tourism, financial services, and high technology.
San Francisco became a hub for technological driven economic growth during the internet boom of the 1990s.
Intense redevelopment towards the "new economy" makes business more technologically minded.
Tourism is one of San Francisco's most important private-sector industries, accounting for over one out of seven jobs in the city.
The city attracts foreign tourists with the fifth-highest number of any U.S. city.
San Francisco has numerous culturally rich streetscapes featuring mixed-use neighborhoods anchored around central commercial corridors.
The Castro is famous as one of the first gay villages in the country.
San Francisco Pride is one of the oldest and largest LGBT pride events in the world.

It was home to the first lesbian-rights organization, Daughters of Bilitis; the first openly gay person to run for public office, José Sarria; and the first openly gay man to be elected to public office in California, Harvey Milk.
The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art houses 20th century and contemporary works of art.

The Fillmore is a music venue located in the Western Addition that gained fame in the 1960s with performances by now-famous musicians such as the Grateful Dead, Janis Joplin, Led Zeppelin, and Jefferson Airplane.
The California Palace of the Legion of Honor holds primarily European antiquities.
The de Young Museum features American decorative pieces and anthropological holdings from Africa, Oceania, and the Americas.
The Asian Art Museum houses Asian art.
The Morrison Planetarium and Steinhart Aquarium are located at the California Academy of Sciences.
Major League Baseball's San Francisco Giants have played in San Francisco since moving from New York in 1958.
The San Francisco 49ers began playing as an All-America Football Conference (AAFC) league charter member, moved to the NFL in 1950 and into Candlestick Park in 1971.
Golden Gate Park is the third most-visited city park in the U.S., after Central Park and the National Mall.

Several of San Francisco's parks and nearly all of its beaches form part of the regional Golden Gate National Recreation Area, one of the most visited units of the National Park system with over 13 million visitors a year.
San Francisco is a charter city and is constituted of two co-equal branches: the executive branch headed by the mayor; and the legislative branch, the Board of Supervisors.
The Supreme Court of California is based in the Earl Warren Building.
Colleges and universities include the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), which operates the UCSF Medical Center.
San Francisco State University is part of the California State University system.
The Academy of Art University is the largest institute of art and design in the nation.
The major daily newspaper in San Francisco is the San Francisco Chronicle.
Sing Tao Daily claims to be the largest of several Chinese language dailies that serve the Bay Area.
San Francisco has nearly 300 preschool programs primarily operated by Head Start, San Francisco Unified School District, private for-profit, private non-profit and family child care providers.
The San Francisco Municipal Railway (Muni) is the primary public transit system of San Francisco.
Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) connects San Francisco with the East Bay and San Jose through the underwater Transbay Tube.
Caltrain runs from San Francisco along the San Francisco Peninsula to San Jose.
Public transportation in San Francisco includes Muni's 69 bus routes, the Muni Metro light rail system, and historic streetcar lines.
Golden Gate Ferries connect the city to North Bay communities, while San Francisco Bay Ferry connects the city to both the North and East Bay.
The Bay Bridge connects the city to Oakland and the East Bay.
State Route 1 enters San Francisco from the north via the Golden Gate Bridge and bisects the city as the 19th Avenue arterial thoroughfare, joining with Interstate 280 at the city's southern border.
In 2014, San Francisco committed to Vision Zero, with the goal of ending all traffic fatalities caused by motor vehicles within the city by 2024.
San Francisco International Airport (SFO) is under the jurisdiction of the City and County of San Francisco.
San Jose International Airport (SJC) is the second-busiest airport in the Bay Area, followed by Oakland International Airport.
Cycling is a popular mode of transportation in San Francisco with 75,000 residents commuting by bicycle each day.
In 2015, Walk Score ranked San Francisco as the second-most walkable city in the United States.
The San Francisco Police Department was founded in 1849.
The San Francisco Fire Department provides both fire suppression and emergency medical services to the city.
San Francisco participates in the Sister Cities program with Shanghai, China.
